pl-l2d27c11-d1e108.summary: States that good use is from virtue and free choice, chiefly virtue, and is among great goods; prevenient grace, a virtue, is not a use of free choice but the source of its good use, from God, not from us; good use is from God and us and so is merit: there God works alone, here God and man.
claims: Grace is from God alone; good use is from God and man.

pl-l2d27c11-d1e111.summary: Cites Augustine on 'by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not void': God first gives grace alone, when only evil merits precede, and then good merits begin through it; 'not void' shows free choice; 'not I, but the grace of God with me,' namely with free choice, shows the will can do nothing good without grace; if grace is lacking, man falls.
claims: Good merits begin only through grace.

pl-l2d27c11.summary: States that the good use is from virtue and from free choice, chiefly from virtue, and counts among great goods. Prevenient grace, a virtue, is not a use of free choice but the source of its good use; it is from God, not from us, while the good use is from God and from us, and so is merit: there God works alone, here God and man. On 'by the grace of God I am what I am,' Augustine says God first gives grace alone where only evil merits precede, and then good merits begin through grace; 'his grace in me was not void' shows free choice; 'not I, but the grace of God with me' shows the will can do nothing good without grace.
claims: Good use comes from virtue and free choice, chiefly virtue.
Prevenient grace is from God alone.
Good use of free choice is from God and from us, and so is merit.
In grace God works alone; in good use God and man work together.
Good merits begin only after grace is given.
If grace is lacking, man falls.
